reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Caused by Rickettsia akari and transmitted by the bite of the house-mouse mite (Liponyssoides sanguineus), with the domestic mouse serving as the reservoir
Classically reported in urban settings with mouse infestations, so a history of living in an apartment block or area with rodents is a useful clue
The illness begins with a painless papule at the mite bite site that evolves into an eschar, appearing before the onset of fever
After an incubation of roughly 7-10 days fever, headache, myalgia and sweats develop, followed by a generalised papulovesicular rash
The vesicular rash can be mistaken for chickenpox, but the presence of an eschar and the epidemiology help distinguish it
Doxycycline produces a rapid response and is the treatment of choice, given empirically on clinical grounds
The disease is characteristically mild and self-limiting, and deaths have not been reported, distinguishing it from the more dangerous spotted fevers
reference.pathophysiology: Rickettsia akari is an obligate intracellular member of the spotted fever group that is introduced into the skin by the feeding mouse mite. It infects vascular endothelium, producing a focal dermal vasculitis at the inoculation site that forms the initial papule and subsequent eschar. Haematogenous dissemination leads to a mild generalised endothelial infection manifesting as the disseminated papulovesicular rash, but the vasculitis is limited in severity, accounting for the benign, self-limiting course.
additionalDifferentials: Papular urticaria or arthropod bite reaction
additionalInvestigations: Indirect immunofluorescence antibody serology with cross-reaction across the spotted fever group
PCR of blood, eschar or a vesicle biopsy
Immunohistochemistry of an eschar or skin biopsy
Full blood count, which may show mild leucopenia
Skin biopsy histology of the eschar or vesicle to demonstrate the characteristic vasculitis
redFlags: Failure of the rash to respond to appropriate therapy, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Widespread haemorrhagic or necrotic lesions, which are atypical and suggest an alternative diagnosis
Severe systemic toxicity, pointing away from rickettsialpox toward a more dangerous rickettsiosis
Immunocompromise altering the expected benign course
reference.prognosis: Rickettsialpox is a benign self-limiting illness that resolves within a week or two even without treatment, and doxycycline shortens the fever; no deaths have been attributed to it.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the vesicular rash as chickenpox and missing the diagnostic eschar
Overlooking the rodent and mite exposure history
Failing to search the skin for the initial eschar
Assuming a benign course means no treatment is warranted when doxycycline hastens recovery
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Give empirical doxycycline on clinical grounds, which produces a rapid response and is the treatment of choice
Offer symptomatic care with antipyretics and analgesia, as the illness is self-limiting even untreated
Reassure regarding the benign course and distinguish the eschar and epidemiology from chickenpox
Undertake rodent and mite control to eradicate mouse infestation and prevent further cases
Confirm with serology, PCR or eschar immunohistochemistry where the diagnosis is uncertain
